analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to share repair information and tools with owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without ever receiving a vote, despite bipartisan sponsorship and 6 cosponsors split evenly between the parties.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern cars are run by onboard computers, and automakers give their franchised dealers the diagnostic information, tools, and software needed to service them. This bill would have required manufacturers to make that same information, tools, and replacement equipment available to car owners and any repair shop on fair, non-discriminatory terms. It protected trade secrets except where the maker already shares the information with dealers. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce it, and states and consumers could sue violators. The bill never got a vote; it died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Car owners, who would be able to get their vehicles fixed at any shop or do the work themselves without being forced back to the dealer for computer-dependent repairs, and independent repair shops and aftermarket parts and tool companies, who could compete on price and quality. The bill's findings note the auto care industry supports roughly 5 million workers in about 495,000 businesses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to provide owners and service providers, on reasonable and non-discriminatory terms, all information needed to diagnose, service, maintain, or repair a vehicle, including all safety alerts, recalls, service bulletins, and anything shared directly or wirelessly with dealers.

Requires manufacturers to offer diagnostic and repair tools for sale to owners and all service providers on fair terms, and to share the information needed for aftermarket companies to make equivalent tools.

Lets consumers and repair shops sue for damages or to enforce compliance, and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents, with the FTC enforcing the requirements as an unfair or deceptive practice.

Protects trade secrets, but bars a manufacturer from withholding information as a trade secret if it already provides that information to authorized dealers or service providers, closing the main loophole that would have made the law toothless.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would bear the cost of making diagnostic information, tools, and replacement equipment available outside their dealer networks, and franchised dealers, whose near-exclusive grip on computer-dependent repair work would face competition from independent shops.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would bear real compliance costs in packaging and distributing diagnostic data, tools, and software, and could pass some of those costs on to new-car buyers.

The bill has a trade-secret exception only where the maker shares information with dealers, but automakers could still argue that releasing repair data and tools exposes intellectual property and could raise concerns about vehicle software security and safety if handled by untrained technicians; the bill leaves the safety question to the repair market rather than setting technician standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real and everyday: owners avoid being locked into dealer pricing for repairs that only dealer-held diagnostic information makes possible. The costs are modest and largely administrative for manufacturers, and the bill carves out genuine trade secrets and defers to the EPA on emissions diagnostics. On balance, the consumer and independent-repair benefits outweigh the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on March 25, 2010, joined by Sen. Sam Brownback, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Six senators cosponsored the bill, three Republicans and three Democrats, giving it bipartisan support from the start.
The Commerce Committee took no further action: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired with the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and franchised dealers kept their exclusive control over diagnostic information and repair tools, and car owners kept paying dealer-side prices for computer-dependent repairs.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Right to Repair Act and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Sam Brownback
for.what_they_did: Joined Boxer in introducing the bill, making it bipartisan from day one.

against.name: Sen. Jay Rockefeller
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Automakers and new-car dealers
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against right-to-repair legislation, arguing dealers needed exclusive access to diagnostic information and that disclosure threatened intellectual property and safety.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and a Republican and drew an even split of cosponsors, 3 Republicans and 3 Democrats, so its death in committee was not a party-line outcome.

industries.note: The bill would have forced manufacturers to share diagnostic information, tools, and software with owners and independent shops, giving up the gatekeeper position that channels computer-dependent repair work to their dealers. Its interest in keeping repair data proprietary runs against owners who want cheaper repair options.

Dealers hold the dealer-held repair information the bill would open up, and their service departments would face direct price competition from independent shops. Their gain from the status quo comes at owners' expense.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and aftermarket parts and tool companies
industries.note: The bill's stated findings note the aftermarket supports about 5 million workers in roughly 495,000 businesses with around $200 billion in annual sales, and it would have guaranteed these shops equal access to the information and tools needed to repair modern cars. Their interest lines up with car owners' interest in competitive repair prices.

Owners would have gotten the legal right to repair information and tools for their own vehicles and to choose where the vehicle's data is sent, instead of being steered back to dealers for computer-controlled systems.
